teach:L3:4: The first thing a seasoned executive does with an impressive number is test it gently.

Then volunteer three caveats before anyone asks: it is an informal estimate, not a controlled comparison; part of the speed is your developer background; the more defensible claim is the method: traceable decisions and reusable playbooks.
you:d3_runsheet: You like structure, and a run-sheet is structure in service of the other person.
Knowing the arc of a 25-minute coffee, his world first, your story briefly, a gift, a question, an early exit, frees you to listen instead of wondering when to bring up the method.
fq:d3_runsheet:0: Why does his world come before your story?
fa:d3_runsheet:0: Because people trust those who are curious about them first, and because I learn what to say by listening.
If I start with Lantern, I am pitching into the dark.
If I start by asking what he is focused on, I can connect my work to his priority in his words.
It also lowers the self-orientation in the trust equation: the meeting feels like it is about his agenda, and my goal emerges from it naturally.
fq:d3_runsheet:1: When do you leave, and why so early?
fa:d3_runsheet:1: Around minute twenty-five to thirty, before he has to end it.
Leaving first shows I respect his time and that I am not trying to extract more from the meeting than he offered.
It also means the coffee ends on a high, with a clear next step, rather than drifting until his assistant arrives.
Executives remember how a meeting ended more than how it started, so I want the last memory to be crisp.
set:d3_coffee: You arrived ten minutes early and took the table facing the wall so he faces the room.
cue:d3_coffee: He arrives, slightly late, phone in hand.
beat:d3_coffee:1: So: I hear you were in Singapore a long time?

beat:d3_coffee:4: Where would something like this matter in my area?

Your Singapore years are a genuine bridge, your evidence is strong, and your risk is talking too much about the work you love.
The talk meter is there for you: aim for about a third of the airtime, ask about his thesis, and leave before he wants you to.
fq:d3_coffee:0: What would you do with more time and a few people?
fa:d3_coffee:0: I would prove the method is not just me.
Take two or three designers and a BA, run it on one real epic for six weeks, and measure discovery-to-sign-off against a baseline.
I would coach them on the job, with a quality gate on every AI output.
If it holds up with other people's hands on it, it is a capability your area can scale.
If it breaks, we learn exactly where, cheaply.
fq:d3_coffee:1: Who else should I be talking to about this?

If you are thinking about lending specifically, Sarah's product owners were the first to ask to try it.
I would be glad to make any of those introductions properly.
cue:d3_about: How did you end up here?

fa:d3_about:0: Partly family, and partly because I could see Vietnam was where the interesting growth was.

fa:d3_about:1: Honestly, not the speed on Lantern, though that is what people notice.

cue:d3_real: A year down to two months.
Honestly, is that real, or is it a slide number?
model:d3_real: It's Ethan's informal estimate, and I think it's fair, here's why: the conventional path for this scope is two designers over roughly two quarters, plus review cycles and rework.
What AI removed was mostly synthesis, documentation and prototype-building time.
The part I'm least sure about is how much transfers to a team that hasn't built the playbooks yet: part of the speed is my developer background.
I'd like to measure it properly on the next epic.
you:d3_real: Risk H1 is rated High for you: about a year is an informal observation and about 60% is your estimate.
This scene is where trust is won or lost.
Saying the caveat before he asks turns a fragile number into proof that you are honest under pressure.
fq:d3_real:0: So how would you prove it properly?
fa:d3_real:0: With a baseline and a second run.
I would take one comparable epic, record how long discovery to sign-off takes the usual way, then run the method with a different team and measure the same thing.
I would also track quality: review rounds and defects after handoff, because speed that creates rework is not speed.
Six weeks would give us a measured number I could stand behind in any room.
fq:d3_real:1: Can I use the number in my deck?
fa:d3_real:1: I'd love you to, with one wording change so it survives questions: one designer, about two months, against a team estimate of about a year.
The year is my manager's informal estimate, not a measured baseline.
If you would like a number that holds up in front of the Group Executive, give me six weeks and I will have a measured comparison.
I would hate for a challenge to land on you.
cue:d3_ai: So what did AI actually do, versus you?
you:d3_ai: False modesty is the quiet backbone habit wearing a different hat.
Saying AI did most of it undersells the judgement that makes your method safe.
This scene trains a precise split: what the tool produced, and what you decided, reviewed and owned.
fq:d3_ai:0: Couldn't anyone with the same tools do this?
fa:d3_ai:0: They could get faster, but not safely.
The tools are available to everyone; what is rare is the method around them.
Deciding what to trust, keeping a decision log for every choice, reviewing every output against the regulation, and packaging it so someone else can repeat it.
Most teams who just use the tools get speed and a pile of confident mistakes.
The method is what turns speed into delivery a bank can sign off.
fq:d3_ai:1: How do you know the AI didn't introduce errors?
fa:d3_ai:1: Every AI output goes through human review against the source: the regulation, the stakeholder's words in the session recording, or the existing system behaviour.
Nothing reaches a decision without a person signing it off in the decision log.
We also track where AI drafts were wrong, so we know which tasks need more checking.
No customer data goes into prompts at all.
The aim is not zero errors from the tool; it is zero unreviewed ones.
you:d3_bill: A small moment with big cultural weight.
You invited, so you host; if he insists, you accept gracefully and promise the next one.
Your Vietnamese and Singaporean instincts both help here: hospitality without a tussle, and a natural reason to meet again.
fq:d3_bill:0: No, no, let me get this one.
fa:d3_bill:0: That's very kind of you, ahn, thank you.
Then the next one is definitely on me, and I'll hold you to it.
Thank you for making the time today; your point about where the bottleneck moves when delivery gets faster really stuck with me.
I'll send you the one-pager on the method tomorrow morning, and I'll let you know how the session with Sarah's team goes.
fq:d3_bill:1: Why not fight harder to pay?
fa:d3_bill:1: Because a long tussle over the bill makes the last minute of the meeting awkward and turns his generosity into a contest.
Offering once, sincerely, shows good manners; accepting gracefully shows I can receive.
Promising the next one creates a light, natural reason to meet again.
In both Vietnamese and Singaporean business culture, that exchange is a small sign of a relationship that will continue.
set:d3_napkin: Back at your desk, you rebuild the about a year argument so it holds up anywhere.
cue:d3_napkin: Order the honest structure for defending any impressive number.
you:d3_napkin: Napkin structure is executive communication in its smallest form: answer, three reasons, ask.
Your scorecard rates executive communication as 3 for evidence and 2 for visibility.
Practising this order until it is automatic is how that score moves.
fq:d3_napkin:0: Why does the answer come before the reasons?
fa:d3_napkin:0: Because a senior listener decides in the first sentence whether to keep listening, and because they may only hear the first sentence.
If I build up to my point, they spend the whole time guessing where I am going.
If I start with it, every reason that follows has somewhere to land.
It also protects me: if I am interrupted after one line, the most important thing has already been said.
fq:d3_napkin:1: What if you don't have three reasons?
fa:d3_napkin:1: Then I give one or two.
Three is a rhythm, not a rule, and padding with a weak third reason undermines the strong two.
Senior people notice when the last point is filler.
I would rather say two reasons and have both land than invent a third.
The structure exists to make thinking visible and easy to follow, not to look complete.
Completeness is my habit; clarity is the goal.
brief:4: Now the part most people skip: the follow-up, the delivery, and the discipline to wait with news instead of chasing.
teach:L4:1: Quote one thing he said, in his words: it proves you listened.
Deliver what you promised before he remembers you promised it.
teach:L4:2: Senior people sort the people below them into three buckets.
Trusted: I can give them a messy problem and it comes back solved, and nothing leaks.
Mine: one of my people; I'll fight for them in talent reviews.
Useful to Trusted: one delivery done impeccably.
Trusted to Mine: repeated delivery plus loyalty under pressure: defending his initiative, telling him bad news early.
teach:L4:3: Every exchange trades information, results, reputation and time.
A healthy relationship gives more than it takes in every currency except reputation, which flows upward first: you make him look good before he spends his name on you.
cue:d4_thanks: At the coffee he said: The bottleneck now is requirements, not code.
You promised a one-pager on the method and to reach out to Sarah about a session for her lending POs.
model:d4_thanks: Thank you for the coffee yesterday, ahn Kai, your point that the bottleneck is now requirements, not code, really stuck with me.
As promised, here's the one-page summary of the method we used on Lantern.

you:d4_thanks: Follow-ups separate people executives remember from people they meet.

Within 24 hours, one line quoting his words, the promised one-pager, and an update on the introduction proves in a single message that you do what you say.
fq:d4_thanks:0: Can you send me more detail on the method?

Whatever format is most useful for you.
fq:d4_thanks:1: Why quote his words back to him?
fa:d4_thanks:1: Because it shows I was listening to him, not waiting for my turn.
Quoting his own point, like where the bottleneck moves when delivery gets faster, tells him the conversation mattered and gives him credit for the idea.
It also makes the message unmistakably personal, not a template.
People remember those who remember what they said, and it is far more convincing than great to meet you.
set:d4_cool: Ethan heard about your coffee from someone else.

fq:d4_cool:0: I just want to know where I stand.
fa:d4_cool:0: That's completely fair, and I'm sorry if this felt like it was happening around you.

Sixty words: what happened, what it means for your time, what you need from him.
It also models the upward reporting that a future manager does every week.

fa:d4_tell:1: Your view on whether the session for Sarah's team fits with our priorities this month.
And, if you are comfortable, your support in principle for me exploring how the method spreads beyond Lantern.
I'm not asking for any change in my role.
I'd just like you in the loop from the start, because the method grew in your team and you should get the credit when it travels.
cue:d4_correct: You realise you told him Ops handle about 5,000 breaks a week.
He just forwarded your one-pager to two of his leads.
you:d4_correct: A number travelling without its caveat is H1 in motion.
Correcting it the same day, in one line, costs you a moment of awkwardness and buys you a reputation for honesty that will matter in every future room where your numbers are challenged.
fq:d4_correct:0: Does that change the story much?
fa:d4_correct:0: Not the direction, just the strength of the claim.
It is still a very large difference, one designer in about two months against a team estimate of about a year.
What changes is how we say it: estimated, not measured.
I would rather we use the careful version now than have someone challenge it later in a bigger room.
And a six-week pilot would give us a measured number to replace it.
fq:d4_correct:1: Why does correcting yourself build trust instead of losing it?
fa:d4_correct:1: Because credibility in the trust equation is about whether your numbers survive questions.
When I correct myself before anyone catches it, I show that my numbers have been checked by the person most likely to want them big.
Executives retell figures upward, and the worst thing that can happen to a sponsor is being embarrassed by a number I gave them.
A quick correction protects him, and he will remember that.
cue:d4_silence: Your session for Sarah's team is booked for next Tuesday.
you:d4_silence: Two quiet weeks after a good coffee feel personal when you have waited a year for a sponsor.
This scene asks you to keep delivering and reconnect with value, not anxiety.
Sponsors notice who stays steady when nothing seems to be happening.
fq:d4_silence:0: What counts as a good reason to reconnect?
fa:d4_silence:0: Something he would be glad to know: a result with one number, an introduction that paid off, or an answer to a question he raised.
Just checking in is about my need; the session with Sarah's team got a 4.6 and two teams want to pilot it is about his interest.
If I have nothing like that yet, I wait and keep working until I do.
News is the best excuse to stay visible.
fa:d4_silence:1: By keeping my attention on the work, not the relationship.
The relationship grows from delivery: every result I produce is a reason for him to remember me.
I also keep a simple log of our interactions and promises, so I can see real progress instead of guessing.
And I remind myself that sponsorship takes months, not weeks.
My job right now is to be reliably useful.
set:d4_howknow: Bao is waiting for the microwave.
cue:d4_howknow: Saw you at the cafe with Kai.
you:d4_howknow: Risk H9: becoming his person too visibly.
Peers notice proximity to power, and Bao is talented and a little competitive.
A modest, true answer that shares credit and invites him in protects relationships you will need when you lead.
fq:d4_howknow:0: So is he going to give you a role?
fa:d4_howknow:0: He saw the Lantern slide and was curious about the method, so we had a coffee and I mostly listened to how his area is thinking about AI.
Honestly, the most useful thing to come out of it is that other teams want to try the method.
I'd love your help with that, actually: you are better than me at prototyping interactions, and I don't want this to be a one-person thing.
fq:d4_howknow:1: Must be nice to have friends in high places.
fa:d4_howknow:1: I get why it looks that way, but really it was one coffee about the work.
What matters to me is that the method spreads, and it won't if it stays attached to my name.
If you're interested, I'd like you to co-run the next session with me; your interaction work would make the prototypes much stronger.
Any credit from it should be shared.
It would make the whole team look good.
cue:d4_log: Keep it private, keep it professional.
Would you be comfortable if he saw your notes?
you:d4_log: You already keep decision logs for every design session.
A relationship log is the same discipline applied to people: dates, his words, promises made, what you learned.
It turns your thoroughness into an asset and keeps you from guessing about where things stand.
fq:d4_log:0: What belongs in the log, and what doesn't?
fa:d4_log:0: Facts and commitments belong: when we met, what he said in his own words, what I promised and by when, what I learned about his priorities, and anything he asked me to keep quiet.
Gossip, guesses about his feelings, and anything I would not want him to read do not.
The test is that the log should be useful and fair if he ever saw it.
It helps me act; it is not a diary.
fq:d4_log:1: How does a log change what you do next?
fa:d4_log:1: It tells me what I owe and when to reconnect.
If I promised a one-pager and an update on Sarah's session, the log shows both are due.
If it has been six weeks since a meaningful touch, it tells me to find news worth sharing.
It also helps me spot patterns, such as which topics make him lean in.
Without it, I would rely on memory and anxiety, which is a poor combination.
set:trap_credit: Anh Kai stops by to see the Lantern prototype.

Vee came up with putting exceptions first.
My part was pushing her on the edge cases, like partial settlements, and helping her test it with two operations users.
That is the part of my work I most want to grow: helping designers like her get to a good answer faster.

brief:5: He once told you he recommended the COO for her role after one.
Three hidden questions will run the whole time.
teach:L5:1: Is this person who I think they are?
(Consistency with the slide and the coffee.) How do they think?
(Judgement, not just skill.) Would I put my name next to theirs?
(Trust, discretion, maturity.) The arc: person 25%, then his world 35%, then the work 20%, then the future 15%, then close with one next step 5%.
Ask about his hard stop at the start and guard his time.
teach:L5:3: If he criticises your manager: don't agree, don't argue: turn it constructive and credit your manager.

cue:d5_questions: Pick the four questions that best show judgement: the how do they think? test.
you:d5_questions: Questions that show judgement are how a senior person assesses you without asking.
Your research background is an advantage: you ask good questions for a living.
Choosing four that reveal how you think about scale, risk and people prepares you for the lunch that decides whether he invests.
fq:d5_questions:0: What do you think the answer is?
fa:d5_questions:0: My guess is that when delivery gets five times faster, the bottleneck moves to decisions: sign-off, risk review and prioritisation.
On Lantern, design and build sped up, but approvals took the same time, so they became the slowest part.
That is why I think the method needs to include governance, not just speed.
I would be curious whether you are seeing the same pattern across Client Platforms.
fq:d5_questions:1: Why prepare questions when the lunch is about you?
fa:d5_questions:1: Because the best way to show how I think is through what I ask.
A good question about where the bottleneck moves, or what makes him confident to give a team ownership, reveals judgement far more than a prepared answer.
It also keeps the conversation balanced, which matters given my tendency to explain at length.
And his answers tell me what he values, which shapes everything I say afterwards.
set:d5_s2: You'll hear this question at lunch.
cue:d5_s2: So: what do you want to do next?
model:d5_s2: On Lantern I've seen what one designer can do with a disciplined AI method.
The next step is making that repeatable through a team, on something that really matters to the bank.
I'd like to do that here.
I'm still working out the best route, so I'd value your view.
you:d5_s2: S2 is the most important thirty seconds in your three weeks.
You have tried for a manager role for over a year; this script states that ambition without demanding a title, ties it to his thesis, and ends with a request for advice.

fq:d5_s2:0: Why do you want to lead?
fa:d5_s2:0: Because the method only matters if it works in other people's hands.
I've seen what one designer can do with it; the bigger impact is a team doing it well, with someone coaching them and keeping the quality bar.
I also enjoy that part: two people I coached now run sessions themselves, and that felt better than my own results.
I want to be accountable for a team's output, not just mine.
fq:d5_s2:1: What makes you think you're ready?
fa:d5_s2:1: I'm ready to lead the work, and partly ready to lead people.

What I haven't done recently is the formal side: hiring, performance conversations, trade-offs across people.
That's exactly the gap I want to close, and I'd rather close it on something that matters than wait for a perfect seat.

Six good questions protect you from accepting a title without the conditions to succeed.
fq:d11_six:0: Which question matters most to you?
fa:d11_six:0: How success is measured in the first year.
Everything else follows from that: whether I'm judged on learner numbers, on adoption in teams, or on business outcomes.
If it's attendance, the role is mostly logistics.
If it's whether teams actually work differently afterwards, it's the role I want.
I'd also want to understand the trainers' development goals, since leading them well is what I'd be accountable for.
fq:d11_six:1: Why ask about the transition from your current work?
fa:d11_six:1: Because how I leave says as much about me as how I arrive.
Lantern and the pilot depend on me, and a sponsor watching will notice whether I leave them in good shape.
Agreeing a transition plan protects Ethan, the team and my reputation.
It also tests the new role: a manager who wants me to start Monday regardless of my commitments may not value reliability.
cue:d11_lateral: I could move you into my area as Lead Designer on the lending portfolio.
Same band, no reports at first.
you:d11_lateral: A lateral move with no reports is close to what your dossier ranks first, but it carries a trap: becoming a great senior IC in a new place.
The leader's answer is enthusiasm plus clarity: agree what six months of success would unlock, and write it down.
fq:d11_lateral:0: What would you want it to unlock?
fa:d11_lateral:0: Concretely, if the lending portfolio delivers the measured improvements we've agreed and the designers I coach can run the method themselves, I'd like to be considered for leading a small team formally.
I'm not asking for a promise today.
I'd just like us both to know what good looks like, so in six months we're having a conversation about evidence rather than hopes.
I'll write it up this week.
fq:d11_lateral:1: He offered you a lateral move?
fa:d11_lateral:1: Yes, and I wanted you to hear it from me first.
It's Lead Designer on the lending portfolio, same band, no reports to start.
If I do, I'd want to plan the Lantern handover properly with you, over a few weeks, so the team isn't exposed.
I'd also really value your view: you know my work better than anyone, and I want to make the right call.
cue:d11_band: And what kind of salary are you expecting?
you:d11_band: Talking about pay is uncomfortable for many people raised to be modest.
The clean answer anchors on scope rather than a number, names the band that matches people leadership, and trusts the process.
It is calm, short, and impossible to read as greedy.
fq:d11_band:0: Do you have a number in mind?
fa:d11_band:0: I'd rather anchor on the role than on a number.
For a people-leader role with four trainers and responsibility for outcomes, I'd expect the Manager band, positioned fairly for my experience.
I trust HR to benchmark that properly.
If the scope changes, for example fewer reports, then I'd expect the band to reflect that too.
What matters most to me is that the role and the band match.
fq:d11_band:1: Why not just name a salary?
fa:d11_band:1: Because a number too low leaves money on the table and a number too high can end the conversation, and I don't have the internal benchmarks.
Naming the band ties my expectation to the scope, which is how the bank thinks about it anyway.
If they come back with a figure, I can then compare it with the band's range and discuss it on evidence rather than feelings.
set:d11_thesis: Bao has heard about both the academy offer and Kai's interest.
cue:d11_thesis: Bao: So which is it: academy, his team, or staying?
Seems like you're applying for everything.
model:d11_thesis: Honestly, it's one thing: I want to lead people in making AI-era ways of working real here: fast and safe.
The academy does that through learning, his team through delivery.
I'm working out which is right first.
you:d11_thesis: Bao's question is the H10 risk said out loud: you're applying for everything.
Your dossier's thesis is the answer: one aim, several routes.
One or two sentences that make you consistent rather than opportunistic will be repeated by peers more than any pitch.
fq:d11_thesis:0: So if both say yes, which one?
fa:d11_thesis:0: Whichever lets me lead people doing the work best, and I'll decide with the advice of people I trust, not by which comes first.
The academy would mean teaching at scale; the delivery role would mean leading a team on real projects.
They're different routes to the same thing.
And whichever I choose, I'd want you involved in the method: you've made it better already.
fq:d11_thesis:1: Why does consistency matter so much to peers?
fa:d11_thesis:1: Because peers decide what people say about you when you are not in the room.
If they think I'm chasing every opportunity, that story reaches managers and sponsors before I do.
One clear thesis that explains every move, making AI-era ways of working real here, safely, turns apparent opportunism into a coherent career.
It also helps me say no to things that don't fit.
set:d11_branch: The last question of the week.
cue:d11_branch: Manager or principal, which do you actually want?
you:d11_branch: Manager or principal: your dossier ranks the player-coach delivery lead first, and the IC principal path a strong second.
The honest answer is the one that matches your best weeks.
Say it plainly, with the reason, and keep your hands on the work.
fq:d11_branch:0: What would you miss if you chose management?
fa:d11_branch:0: Probably the deep work: the hours of building a prototype until it's right.
I'd keep some of that as a player-coach, but less.
What I'd gain is the thing I already enjoy most: seeing someone I coached ship something better than I would have.
I've noticed my best weeks are those weeks.
So I'd rather trade some craft time for that, and keep enough hands-on work to stay credible.
fq:d11_branch:1: And if principal turned out to be the better fit?
fa:d11_branch:1: Then I'd want to know, and I'd take it seriously.
A principal role would let me shape how the whole bank designs with AI, which is also meaningful work.
I'd still want to grow people through it, by mentoring and setting standards.
If after six months you or Ethan see me thriving more on the IC side, I'd rather adjust than hold onto a title.
The goal is impact, not a label.
set:trap_suckup: Anh Kai, Min Chow and Chee Lan around the table.
cue:trap_suckup: Kai: What if we put an AI chatbot on every lending form by Q 1?
you:trap_suckup: You are early in Kai's orbit, and the temptation to agree loudly is strongest now.
But he spotted you for a method that is fast and honest.
Flattery would make you look like a fan, not a future leader, and Chow and Lan would quietly mark you down for it.
fq:trap_suckup:0: Do you think the chatbot idea is a good one?
fa:trap_suckup:0: I think the direction is right, and I would test it before scaling it.
On Lantern we saw AI help on simple fields but confuse people on complex ones, so I would expect mixed results across forty forms.
If we pilot the guarantee form for four weeks and measure completion time and errors against today, we will know where it works.
I can draft that measure plan by Wednesday.
fq:trap_suckup:1: You challenged him in front of us.
fa:trap_suckup:1: But I did not really challenge him; I offered one data point and a way to make his idea succeed.
Agreeing with everything would have been easier and less useful.
Leaders get flattery all day, and it can push them into big calls without the facts.
I would rather be the person who helps him get it right.
And I would value your view on how the forms should feel.
brief:12: Day one in the new role.
Your path shapes the week: people who report to you, or people you must lead without reports.
teach:L12:1: Week 1: agree your manager's expectations, his goals, pressures and how he likes information (Gabarro and Kotter, again).
Weeks 1-2: a 1:1 with every person: goals, frustrations, what they need from you.
By day 45: one visible quick win.
teach:L12:2: Three traps you are specifically prone to.
Doing the work yourself because you're faster with AI: your job is now to make them fast.
Over-explaining in 1:1s: ask more, tell less.
Avoiding hard feedback to keep harmony.
Gallup: managers account for at least 70% of the variance in team engagement.
That is why sponsors are careful whom they make managers.
set:d12_expect: Day one in the new role.
A message to Kai, now your manager.
cue:d12_expect: You want 30 minutes this week to agree his expectations for your first 90 days.
model:d12_expect: Anh Kai, could I have 30 minutes this week to agree what success looks like for my first 90 days?
I'd like to understand your goals and pressures for the lending portfolio, and how you prefer to hear from me.
I'll bring a one-page draft for you to tear up.
you:d12_expect: New managers fail most often by guessing what their boss wants.
You are a researcher: treat Kai as your first user in the new role.
Asking for thirty minutes to agree ninety-day expectations, with a draft he can tear up, is the habit that keeps a sponsor turned manager on your side.
fq:d12_expect:0: What do you think success looks like?
fa:d12_expect:0: Delivery: the lending portfolio hits the dates we've agreed, with the method measured against a baseline.
People: the designers I lead can run the method without me, and I've had at least one hard conversation well.
Relationships: Sarah's team and Risk trust our work enough to ask for more.
I'd like you to tell me what's missing and what matters most to you.
fq:d12_expect:1: How often do you want to meet?
fa:d12_expect:1: Whatever suits you, but I'd suggest thirty minutes every two weeks for the first ninety days, plus a three-line update every Friday so you never need to chase me.
If something is going wrong, you'll hear it the same day, not at our next one-on-one.
And I'd value one honest piece of feedback from you each month, since that's how I'll get better fastest in a new role.
set:d12_tour: Your first 1:1 with Dat, now formally in your team.
cue:d12_tour: He arrives with a notebook and sits very straight.
beat:d12_tour:1: The deadlines are a bit... tight sometimes.
beat:d12_tour:2: What do you need from me as your manager? you ask.
you:d12_tour: Your first one-on-one as a formal manager.
Your coaching instincts are strong; the shift is listening without fixing.
Dat is proud and quietly struggling.
A listening tour that asks about his goals and what gets in his way builds the trust you will need for the hard conversation later.
fq:d12_tour:0: What do you expect from me?
fa:d12_tour:0: Good work, honesty about problems early, and that you tell me what you need to grow.
I'd like us to agree two or three goals together in the next couple of weeks, based on what you want, not just what the project needs.
I'll give you feedback regularly, good and hard, and I'd like you to do the same for me.
I'm new at this too, so tell me when I get it wrong.
fq:d12_tour:1: Why ask questions instead of setting the agenda?
fa:d12_tour:1: Because the first one-on-one tells him what kind of manager I am.
If I talk most of the time, he learns this is a place for instructions.
If I ask about his goals, what he enjoys and what gets in his way, he learns it is his time.
I also learn things a project plan never shows, like what motivates him and what might be going on outside work.
That is the information a manager actually needs.
cue:d12_vy: Vee: I'm stuck on the lending upload flow.
You can see the answer in ten seconds.
model:d12_vy: Which of the three would you pick if I weren't here, and why?
What would a banker on a slow connection need most from it?
Try your pick with one PO and show me Thursday?
you:d12_vy: You can see the answer in ten seconds, and that is exactly the trap.
Your dossier says you are a great teacher; managers grow people by asking.
Two or three questions, and no answers, turns Vee into someone who can solve the next one without you.
fq:d12_vy:0: Can't you just tell me which one is right?
fa:d12_vy:0: I could give you my opinion, but then you'd be designing for me rather than for the banker.
And honestly, you know this flow better than I do now.
Tell me which you'd pick if I weren't here, and why.
If we disagree, we'll test both with one PO.
What I really want is for you to trust your own judgement, because in three months you'll be making these calls without me.
fq:d12_vy:1: When is it right to just give the answer?
fa:d12_vy:1: When the stakes are high and time is short, or when the person is completely new and has nothing to reason from.
A production incident is not a coaching moment.
But a design choice with a day to spare is exactly where learning happens.
My rule is: if they can probably get there with a question or two, I ask.
If they can't, I explain my reasoning, not just my answer, so next time they can.
set:d12_delegate: Vee's draft of the lending flow is 70% there.
cue:d12_delegate: You could fix it yourself with AI in forty minutes.
you:d12_delegate: Fixing it yourself in forty minutes is the habit that kept you a brilliant individual contributor.
Writing three clear comments and offering fifteen minutes in the morning is slower tonight and faster for the next year.
This is the manager trade-off in its purest form.
fq:d12_delegate:0: Sorry, I should have done better.
Should I stay late to fix it?
fa:d12_delegate:0: No need to stay late, and no need to apologise: seventy percent is a solid draft.
I've sent you three specific comments; they should take about an hour.
Go home, rest, and let's meet at eight thirty to go through them together before the review.
If something doesn't make sense, that's my fault for explaining badly, not yours.
I'd rather you present your own work tomorrow than mine.
fq:d12_delegate:1: What if the review goes badly because you didn't fix it?
fa:d12_delegate:1: Then it goes slightly worse than it could have, and Vee learns far more than if I had rescued it.
I'd prepare her so the risk is small: specific comments tonight, fifteen minutes in the morning, and I'd be in the room to support her.
If a stakeholder raises something we missed, I'd own it with her.
A slightly imperfect review she leads is better than a perfect one she watches.
set:d12_standard: You want five teams to adopt the AI quality gate, and you manage none of them.
cue:d12_standard: Lan: Why should my leads adopt your gate?
you:d12_standard: Influence without authority is most of a lead's job.
You built the quality gate; now you need five teams who report to other people to adopt it.
Leading with what it gives Lan's leads, and inviting them to cut parts of it, is how standards spread without a mandate.
fq:d12_standard:0: And if my leads think it's just more process?
fa:d12_standard:0: Then I want to hear exactly which parts feel like process, and we'll cut them.
The gate has six checks; maybe four matter for their work.
The point isn't compliance, it's that AI-generated work gets reviewed where it's riskiest, so designers spend time on judgement rather than rework.
If two of your leads try it on one feature and say it slowed them down, I'll take that back and change it.
fa:d12_standard:1: I'd suggest the chapter owns it, with you as the sponsor, and I maintain it.
It came out of the chapter's work, and it should be the chapter's standard, not mine or Client Platforms's.
If your leads change it, the change goes in with their names.
That way it becomes something the chapter is proud of, rather than something imposed from outside.
I'd value you presenting it at the next design forum.
set:d12_mentor: Vee isn't your report, but Kai wants evidence you grow people.
cue:d12_mentor: You want to offer Vee a structured mentorship: a written goal, monthly check-ins, and a 3-month review.
model:d12_mentor: Would a bit of structured mentoring be useful?
We'd pick one goal you care about, write it down, meet once a month, and look back after three months.
No pressure at all: happy either way.
you:d12_mentor: Kai wants evidence that you grow people.
You have mentored more than fifty people informally; structured mentoring with a written goal and a three-month review turns that generosity into evidence a panel can see.
Keep the offer light, specific and easy to decline.
fq:d12_mentor:0: What kind of goal do you mean?
fa:d12_mentor:0: Something you care about that would make your work better in three months.
For example, presenting to POs with confidence, or leading a stakeholder workshop on your own, or getting faster at the method.
We'd write it in a sentence, agree what good looks like, and check in once a month.
After three months we look back honestly.
If it isn't helping, we stop, no hard feelings.
fa:d12_mentor:1: Because structure makes progress visible, to her and to anyone assessing my leadership.
Informal help is kind, but it leaves no trace and often drifts.
A written goal, monthly check-ins and a review give her a sense of momentum and give me evidence of developing others, which my dossier says is the gap.
It also respects her time: she knows exactly what she's signing up for.
set:d12_report45: Forty-five days since the ask: compressed into a week of game time.
cue:d12_report45: You promised to report on two things: hard feedback and growing someone.
So far: one S B I conversation with Dat (planned for Monday), and Vee is coached weekly and presented to the POs.
model:d12_report45: Day-45 update on hard feedback and growing someone.
Growing someone: Vee has weekly coaching and presented the lending flow to the POs herself.
Hard feedback: my first S B I conversation is Monday, not done yet.
you:d12_report45: You promised a forty-five day report, and one of the two things is not done yet.
Reporting honestly on the gap, with a date, is stronger than waiting until both are complete.
This is the reliability habit applied to your own development.
fq:d12_report45:0: Why hasn't the feedback conversation happened yet?
fa:d12_report45:0: Honestly, I delayed it a week to collect specific examples, and I was nervous about getting it right.
I now have two clear examples from the last fortnight, and it's booked for Monday morning.
I've prepared it using S B I and I'll ask for his view first.
I'll tell you how it went in my Friday update.
I know delaying hard conversations is a habit I need to break as a manager.
fa:d12_report45:1: Six weeks ago she froze when a PO challenged her.
Last week she presented the lending flow herself, handled two tough questions, and only looked at me once.
Our weekly coaching focused on preparing for the hardest question rather than the whole presentation.
Her next goal is running a stakeholder workshop alone.
I'd love you to see her present at the next review.
set:trap_cc: The API spec from Min Chow's team is three days late and blocking Lantern testing.
cue:trap_cc: Your cursor hovers over the CC field.
you:trap_cc: Your profile shows you are steady with operations and engineering partners, and Lantern depends on them.
A punitive CC would win one deadline and lose Chow for the rest of the project.
It would also show Kai that you escalate before you talk to people.
fa:trap_cc:0: Because escalating first would have told you I did not trust you, and I needed your help more than your fear.
I assumed there was a reason, and there was: two people out sick.
Writing the field list was a small price for a spec two days later.
If it had slipped again, I would have asked you to raise it with me, together, not around you.
Thanks for turning it round so quickly.
fq:trap_cc:1: When is copying a senior person actually right?
fa:trap_cc:1: When they need the information to make a decision, not when I want to apply pressure.
If a delay changes a date that an executive has promised someone, I tell them directly, ideally with the other person, and with a plan.
The test I use is simple: would I be comfortable if the other person knew why I added the name?
If the honest answer is to make them look bad, I take it out.
brief:13: Dat has missed two handoff details in two weeks.
Kai has some feedback for you, too.
And you're on your first hiring panel.
teach:L13:1: S B I and Radical Candor.
Situation, In Tuesday's handoff for the lending form...
Behaviour,...the error states for the three upload fields weren't in the file...
Impact,...so engineering built without them and we lost two days.
Kim Scott: care personally, challenge directly.
Silence to keep harmony is ruinous empathy: it feels kind and isn't.
teach:L13:2: When you are on the receiving end.
Blunt negative feedback from a sponsor is a gift.
Thank them, clarify with one example, change, and report back in 4-6 weeks.
And when asked to say a few words without warning: prep: Point, Reason, Example, Point.
teach:L13:3: Affinity bias: liking people who remind you of you.
The halo effect: one strength colouring everything.
The cure is boring and works: the same questions, the same evidence, written down before you compare candidates.
set:d13_sbi_sort: Your notes for a feedback conversation with Dat.
cue:d13_sbi_sort: Sort each line: Situation, Behaviour, Impact, or Not feedback (judgement or label).
you:d13_sbi_sort: Feedback that labels people (careless, not committed) damages trust; feedback that describes behaviour builds it.
Sorting lines into Situation, Behaviour, Impact and not feedback trains you to hear the difference before you say something you cannot take back.
fa:d13_sbi_sort:0: Because it is a judgement about his state of mind, not a description of something he did.
He can argue with it, feel accused, and still not know what to change.
In Tuesday's handoff, the error states for three fields weren't in the file is a fact he can check and act on.
Feedback should describe what a camera would have seen, then the impact, then ask for his view.
fq:d13_sbi_sort:1: Why ask for his view after the impact?
fa:d13_sbi_sort:1: Because I don't know the whole story.
There may be a reason I can't see: unclear requirements, too much work, something at home.
Asking for his view turns a verdict into a conversation and lets him keep his dignity.
It also tells me whether this is a skill problem, a workload problem or a personal one, and each needs a different response from me as his manager.
set:d13_sbi: Dat has missed two handoff details in two weeks.
cue:d13_sbi: Behaviour: the error states for the three upload fields weren't in the file.
Impact: engineering built without them; two days lost.
model:d13_sbi: I want to raise something because I value your work.
In Tuesday's lending handoff, the error states for the three upload fields weren't in the file, so engineering built without them and we lost two days.
What's your view of what happened?
you:d13_sbi: Your dossier names performance conversations as the decisive gap for a manager role.
Your warmth is a strength; the risk is softening it until the point disappears.
Open with why you are raising it, describe the behaviour precisely, name the impact, then ask.
fa:d13_sbi:0: I'm not looking for an apology though; I'd like to understand what happened so we can make it easy to get right.
Was it the handoff checklist, the deadline, or something else?
It's not like you, which is why I wanted to ask.
Whatever it is, let's fix the cause together.
And if anything is making work harder at the moment, I'd like to know.
fq:d13_sbi:1: I've had a lot going on at home.
fa:d13_sbi:1: Thank you for telling me; I'm sorry it's been hard.
You don't need to share details.
Let's look at what would help: we could lighten your load for a few weeks, move a deadline, or I can pair someone with you on handoffs.
And there's confidential support through the employee programme if that would be useful.
The handoff still matters, so let's find a way that works for you right now.
cue:d13_receive: Honest feedback, since you asked for it: in meetings you explain too much before you get to the point.
People tune out by your second minute.
you:d13_receive: This is your own feedback, said aloud by your sponsor: you explain too much before the point.
The test is not whether it stings; it is whether you can thank him, ask for one example, and commit to a change with a date.
Receiving feedback well is a leadership signal.
fq:d13_receive:0: You're not going to defend yourself?
fa:d13_receive:0: No, because you're right, and I've heard it before from a peer.
I think it comes from wanting to be complete.
I'd rather fix it than explain it.
I'm going to start every update with the headline in one sentence and then stop, and let people ask for more.
Would you be willing to tell me in a month whether you've noticed a difference?
fq:d13_receive:1: Why ask for an example instead of agreeing straight away?
fa:d13_receive:1: Because a specific example tells me exactly what to change, and it shows I'm taking the feedback seriously rather than nodding politely.
In Tuesday's meeting you spent two minutes on background before the decision is something I can practise.
Agreeing immediately can sound like I just want the conversation to end.
Asking for one example, then thanking him, shows I want to learn.
set:d13_prep: Kai, without warning: Min, say a few words about the pilot?
model:d13_prep: My one point: AI makes design faster, but the real gain is better decisions earlier.
On the lending pilot, the POs reacted to a running prototype in week two, not week ten: Vee ran those sessions.
So my suggestion for everyone here: prototype early, decide early.
you:d13_prep: An unplanned say a few words is where your compression work shows. prep, point, reason, example, point, gives you a shape in five seconds.
Crediting Vee by name in front of forty people is visibility for her and a leadership signal for you.
fq:d13_prep:0: What was the hardest part of the pilot?
fa:d13_prep:0: The method worked faster than the organisation around it, so Risk approval became the bottleneck.
We learned to start access requests in week zero, and Raj's team now has a template for it.
It's a good example of where the bottleneck moves when design gets faster: to decisions and controls.
That's the next thing worth solving.
fq:d13_prep:1: Why name Vee in front of everyone?
fa:d13_prep:1: Because specific public credit is the cheapest and most powerful thing a leader can give.
It costs me a few words and gives her visibility she couldn't get on her own.
It also tells forty people that I build people up, which is exactly the evidence my dossier says I need.
And it's true: she ran those sessions.
Leaders who share credit find that more of it comes back to them.
set:d13_hire: Debrief after two designer interviews, with Chee Ha, HR Business Partner.
cue:d13_hire: Candidate A trained in Singapore like you, was charming, and showed one brilliant AI prototype.
Candidate B was nervous but answered every structured question with specific evidence.
you:d13_hire: Hiring is the manager skill you have least evidence for.
Candidate A is like you: Singapore-trained, charming, AI-brilliant.
Scoring both against the same questions before deciding is what fair, evidence-based hiring looks like, and Ha will notice.
fa:d13_hire:0: I understand why: A was engaging and the prototype was impressive.
But we agreed the five questions in advance because they predict success in the role, and on those B was stronger on four of five, with specific examples.
A's prototype is one data point.
I'd also flag that A shares my background, so I want to be careful I'm not favouring someone like me.
I'd recommend B, and offer A feedback.
fq:d13_hire:1: How do you notice your own bias in the moment?
fa:d13_hire:1: I ask myself what I liked before I ask what they showed.
If the answer is they reminded me of me, that is a warning.
Charm, a shared school or a similar career path make interviews feel easy, which is not the same as evidence.
Scoring each answer against the same criteria, before discussing, forces me to compare evidence.
Then I check whether my overall feeling matches the scores.
cue:d13_candor: Sort each manager line into its quadrant.
you:d13_candor: Kim Scott's quadrants matter for someone as warm as you: the most common new-manager failure is ruinous empathy, caring so much you never say the hard thing.
Sorting real manager lines teaches you to care personally and challenge directly in the same sentence.
fq:d13_candor:0: Which quadrant are you most likely to fall into?
fa:d13_candor:0: I care about people and I dislike conflict, so my risk is softening feedback until it is useless, or delaying it.
My forty-five day report already showed that: I postponed the conversation with Dat.
The fix is to remember that withholding feedback is not kind; it lets someone fail without knowing why.
Caring personally means saying the hard thing, clearly and soon.
fq:d13_candor:1: What does radical candour sound like for you?
fa:d13_candor:1: Something like: I want to raise this because I think you can do much better work, and I want you to get the credit for it.
In Tuesday's handoff, the error states were missing, and engineering lost two days.
It starts with genuine care, describes the behaviour precisely, names the impact, and invites his view.
Warm and direct at the same time.
set:trap_afterparty: Teams, five minutes after Chee Lan closed the design review.
Everyone agreed to her navigation direction.
cue:trap_afterparty: Bao in a side chat: That direction is so dated.
Let's just build ours in the prototype.
you:trap_afterparty: Lan is the Craft Guardian who wants to be consulted before, not informed after.
Agreeing in her review and building something else behind it is the precise opposite.
You need her support for anything design-led you propose, and she will remember who went around her.
fq:trap_afterparty:0: Why bring me the concern instead of just building it your way?
fa:trap_afterparty:0: Because it is your decision, and you can only make a good one if you hear the doubts.

cue:d14_star: Tell me about a time you developed someone.

I set one goal with her, present to the POs herself, and I asked questions in our weekly 1:1s instead of giving answers.

fa:d14_star:0: For the first two reviews I answered questions for her when she hesitated, because I wanted it to go well.

cue:d14_presence: Pick the three habits that most raise presence for a quiet, competent person.

brief:15: Rumours of a merger, two sponsors who disagree, and a lift ride where Kai asks something he shouldn't.

teach:L15:1: Be the bridge, not the battlefield.

set:trap_screenshot: Bao and three others are venting about Ethan's new 45-minute stand-up.

brief:16: Something is going on that he hasn't told anyone.
And you are running on empty.
teach:L16:1: Care first, clarity second, plan third.
Care: stop, acknowledge, ask what he needs right now.
Clarity: still say plainly what has been happening with the work and why it matters.
Plan: agree together what changes, scope, dates, support (flexible hours, leave, the employee assistance programme via HR), and when you'll check in.
Involve HR for options, not as a threat.
Keep what he told you private; share only what others need to know to support the plan.
teach:L16:2: Psychological safety (Edmondson) is the belief that you won't be punished for speaking up.
It isn't comfort; it is what makes candour possible.

set:d16_notice: He's been arriving late and leaving at 17:00 exactly.

fq:d16_notice:0: Why did you say it was on you in the channel?

I'm not here to blame you.
I'd like us to work out together what would make the handoffs land, and what you need from me.
fq:d16_notice:1: Why not wait until the end of the week to talk?

Engineering is already frustrated, and Dat probably knows something is wrong and is worrying about it.
Talking the same day, privately, shows I take both the work and him seriously.
Delaying hard conversations is the habit my forty-five day report exposed.
Leaders who act early have kinder conversations.
set:d16_order: One hour before your conversation with Dat.
cue:d16_order: Put the conversation in the right order.
you:d16_order: A hard conversation needs a shape so that care and clarity both survive your nerves.

fq:d16_order:0: Why ask how he's doing before the facts?

Asking first gives him the chance to share, and shows I see him as a person, not a missed deadline.
But I keep it short and sincere, then name the purpose clearly so he isn't waiting for the other shoe to drop.
Care first, then clarity, then his view, then a plan.
fq:d16_order:1: What makes the expectation clear rather than vague?

Every handoff includes error states and a checklist, starting this Friday, and we'll review the next two together is clear.

Clear expectations are kind: they remove guessing.

cue:d16_open: You want to open in a way that is both caring and clear, he should know this is about the work, and that you're on his side.
model:d16_open: I wanted to talk about the last few weeks of handoffs, because it's not like you and I want to help.
Before anything else: how are you doing?
you:d16_open: The first sentence of a hard conversation decides whether the person hears it as care or as a verdict.
Two sentences: why you are talking, that you are on his side, and a genuine question.

fa:d16_open:0: Yes, it is, and I want to be straight with you.

brief:17: Your week spans Ho Chi Minh City, a Singapore-trained executive and a GM in Melbourne.
teach:L17:1: Respect in form, crispness in content, candour in bad news.
Vietnam: hierarchy and face matter; yes often means I heard you; bad news is softened.
Singapore: direct, efficient, data-first; yes usually means yes.
Australia: low hierarchy, first names, understatement; bad news expected early; maybe means no; over-selling is disliked.
The rule for a Vietnam-based leader: Vietnamese respect in form, Singapore crispness in content, Australian candour in bad news.
teach:L17:2: To a Risk Guardian or an Australian sceptic, speed sounds like risk.
Lead with traceability: Speed is the side effect; what we optimised for was auditability, every decision links to its source.
And if a data or privacy concern about your AI tooling is raised: in a bank, pause first, explain second.
Stop the practice in question, engage Risk, document what data went where.
teach:L17:3: Read the archetype from the first question.
