What's the headline?: Group Executive: one story, one number.
set:d17_diag: Your calendar this week is mostly people you've never met.
cue:d17_diag: Sort each first question into the archetype it signals.
you:d17_diag: As you move up, most of your calendar becomes people you have never met.
Reading the archetype from someone's first question, a Risk Guardian, a Visionary, an Overloaded Operator, lets you adapt in minutes.
You are a researcher; this is user research done live.
fq:d17_diag:0: What do you do if you misread someone's archetype?
fa:d17_diag:0: If I lead with a big vision and they keep asking about controls, I've misread a Risk Guardian as a Visionary, so I switch to traceability and data handling.
The archetype is a hypothesis, not a label.
I watch their reactions: what makes them lean in, what makes them check their phone.
Being willing to change approach mid-conversation matters more than guessing right first time.
fq:d17_diag:1: Which archetype do you find hardest?
fa:d17_diag:1: Probably the Overloaded Operator, because my instinct is to explain thoroughly and they have no time for it.
With them I need the headline in one sentence, the decision I need, and nothing else.
Anything more feels like a burden.
The irony is that they're often the most important people for getting things done, so compressing for them is a skill worth practising daily.
set:d17_lens: The same news, the pilot slips two weeks, written three ways.
cue:d17_lens: Sort each version to the audience it fits best.
you:d17_lens: Your cross-cultural range is rated 5 for evidence and 2 for visibility.
Singapore, Vietnam and Australia all hear the same bad news differently.
Sorting three versions of one message to the right audience is how you turn a hidden strength into everyday credibility.
fq:d17_lens:0: How does the same news change for Melbourne versus Vietnam?
fa:d17_lens:0: For Melbourne, plain and direct: We're two weeks behind, here's why, here's the plan, with a little informality and no padding.
For a senior Vietnamese leader, the same facts but more care with face: private first, respectful address, and the ownership framed so nobody looks bad in front of others.
The facts never change; the delivery does.
fq:d17_lens:1: Isn't adapting your style a bit fake?
fa:d17_lens:1: No more than speaking slower to someone in their second language is fake.
The substance and honesty stay identical; I'm choosing the delivery that lets the message land.
Refusing to adapt is actually less respectful, because it makes the listener do all the work.
Having lived in Singapore and Vietnam and worked with Australia, I can do this naturally.
It's an advantage I should use more visibly.
set:d17_au: It's her Tuesday morning in Melbourne.
cue:d17_au: The lending copilot concept is two weeks behind because your team's first prototype failed usability with three bankers.
You've already re-planned: a simpler flow tested Friday.
model:d17_au: Hi Sarah, heads-up: the lending copilot is about two weeks behind.
Our first prototype didn't work for your bankers in testing, which is on us.
We've simplified the flow and we're testing it with three bankers Friday.
you:d17_au: Sarah wants plain English and bad news early.
Your instinct may be to explain the usability findings in full.
Australian directness is the right register: what is late, why, that it is on you, the new plan, an open door.
fq:d17_au:0: What went wrong with the bankers?
fa:d17_au:0: The first prototype tried to do too much.
It showed every field from the application on one screen, and in testing all three bankers struggled to find the loan amount and the risk flags quickly.
That's on us: we designed for completeness instead of their real task.
The new flow shows the three things they check first and hides the rest.
We'll know on Friday if it works.
fq:d17_au:1: Is two weeks the real number, or will it slip again?
fa:d17_au:1: Two weeks is my honest estimate, and I'd put it at about eighty percent.
The risk is that Friday's test also fails, which would add another week.
If that happens, you'll hear from me on Friday afternoon, not at the next steering committee.
I'd rather tell you early than surprise you.
If it passes, we're back on the revised plan, and I'll confirm the date in writing.
set:d17_raj: You came to discuss the AI summariser.
you:d17_raj: Raj is a Risk Guardian: controls first, documentation, data handling.
Leading with speed would confirm his fears.
Your method is genuinely built for traceability, so lead with that and invite him to inspect the decision log.
That is how Risk becomes your strongest reference.
fq:d17_raj:0: What happens when the summary is wrong?
fa:d17_raj:0: The banker sees the source page alongside every summary line, so a wrong line is easy to spot and check.
A human reviews every output before it's used in a decision, and any correction is logged, so we can see how often and where the tool gets it wrong.
If errors cross a threshold we agree with your team, we pause it.
I'd like you to set that threshold, not me.
fq:d17_raj:1: Why should I trust a designer on controls?
fa:d17_raj:1: You shouldn't trust me on my word, and I'd rather you didn't.
That's why I'm asking you to review the decision log for one real application yourself.
The method was built in a regulated workflow and every design choice traces to its source, which is unusual.
But you know the failure modes far better than I do.
If you find gaps, I'd rather fix them before anything goes near production.
cue:d17_privacy: A designer on your team pasted real customer names into a public AI tool last week.
you:d17_privacy: A privacy incident involving someone you lead is a test of honesty under pressure, and of protecting your team without hiding facts.
Confirm it, contain it, document it, and ask for Risk's guidance.
How you handle this will define how Raj sees you for years.
fq:d17_privacy:0: Why did your designer think that was acceptable?
fa:d17_privacy:0: Because the guidance on public AI tools wasn't clear when she did it, and I hadn't explained it to my team.
She used it once, before the guidance came out, and told me as soon as I asked.
I've paused the tool, I'm documenting exactly what data went where, and I'll run a short session for the whole team today on what's allowed.
fa:d17_privacy:1: You made a mistake, and we'll handle it properly together, but you're not in trouble with me.
The guidance wasn't clear and I hadn't briefed the team, which is on me.
What I need from you is to help me document exactly what you pasted and when, honestly, by eleven.
Risk may want to talk to you; I'll be there with you.
Thank you for being straight when I asked.
set:d17_maybe: End of a video call with Sarah.
cue:d17_maybe: You asked if she'd sponsor a second pilot with her bankers.
Let's see how the copilot goes.
you:d17_maybe: Yeah, maybe is a polite no in many cultures, and Australians use it too.
Your instinct may be to accept it and move on.
Naming it kindly, it sounds like you're not convinced yet, and asking what she would need, turns a dead end into a requirement.
fq:d17_maybe:0: I need to see the copilot work first.
fa:d17_maybe:0: That's completely fair, and I'd rather earn it than push.
Let's park the second pilot until the copilot proves itself.
I'll send you the Friday test results, and if the bankers can use it without help, I'll ask you again with the evidence.
If they can't, you'll hear that from me too.
Is there one measure that would convince you, like time saved per application?
fq:d17_maybe:1: Why not just wait for her to raise it again?
fa:d17_maybe:1: A vague maybe usually fades into a no without anyone saying so, and I'd never learn why.
Naming it gently gives her permission to tell me her real concern, which turns guessing into a clear requirement.
It also shows I can hear indirect signals, which senior stakeholders value.
Then I can deliver exactly what would change her mind.
set:trap_kickdown: Michael, visiting from Australia, arrives in ten minutes for the Lantern demo.
cue:trap_kickdown: Vee's demo file still shows last week's numbers.
you:trap_kickdown: You are trying to prove you can lead people, and executive visits are exactly when that is tested.
How you treat Vee with Michael ten metres away is the evidence.
Snapping down while smiling up is the one habit that makes senior people quietly decide you are not manager material.
fa:trap_kickdown:0: It was a small miss, and you fixed it in time, which is what matters.
The real problem is that we had no checklist, and that is on me as much as you.
Let's build a five-point pre-demo list together this afternoon.
And you answered Michael's question about the filter really well.
I would like you to present that part yourself next time someone senior visits.
fq:trap_kickdown:1: Michael said you were calm with the team.
fa:trap_kickdown:1: Ten minutes before he arrived, we found last week's numbers in the demo file.
I asked Vee to update them while I checked the flow, and opened with the story to buy time.
It worked, and she handled his question about the filter better than I would have.
We have since made a short pre-demo checklist, so it should not happen again.
I will share it with the team on Monday.
brief:18: The project is red, Sarah is sceptical, Raj wants controls, and Michael has invited you to dinner.
teach:L18:1: The room is for the recovery plan. bluff R privately beforehand, to each person who could be surprised.
In the room: one line on status, one on cause, then the recovery plan and the one decision you need.
Nobody wants the excuse; everybody wants the plan.
teach:L18:2: When a Group Executive asks it, give one story, one number, and make your own executive look good.
Kai pushed us to prove it on a real lending epic: 6 weeks versus 14, measured.
And your peers: today's peer is tomorrow's sponsor or blocker.
Help them succeed in front of seniors.
set:d18_peer: Bao now manages a peer team.
You're both presenting in Melbourne this week.
cue:d18_peer: Bao: Your slot is right before mine.
Mine's about our design-system work: overlaps a bit with yours.
you:d18_peer: Bao is now a peer manager, and overlapping slots in Melbourne could make you rivals in front of the people who matter.
Offering to co-present his part, with credit to him, turns competition into alliance.
Peers who trust you become the backbone of a senior career.
fq:d18_peer:0: Won't that make your slot weaker?
fa:d18_peer:0: I think it makes both stronger.
The audience will see one connected story instead of two teams overlapping, and your design-system work is genuinely what made our flows reusable, so they should hear it from you.
Let's spend thirty minutes tonight aligning slides: I'll cut my overlap and hand you the bridge.
Melbourne will remember a joined-up Vietnam design team far more than either of us alone.
fq:d18_peer:1: Why invest in a peer who might compete with you?
fa:d18_peer:1: Because peers become the people who run the teams I need to work with, and the people who talk about me when I'm not there.
Competing with Bao in Melbourne might win me one good slot; allying with him wins years of cooperation.
Senior leaders also notice who makes others look good.
Generosity with peers is strategic, but it only works if it's genuine.
set:d18_prewire: Melbourne, the evening before steering committee.
cue:d18_prewire: The lending copilot is red: the second usability round passed, but the integration with the loan system will miss the March release by four weeks.
Cause: an API dependency you assumed was ready: you didn't check early enough.
Plan: ship the summary panel standalone in March, integrate in April.
Ask: her support for the standalone release.
model:d18_prewire: Hi Sarah, before tomorrow's steering committee: the copilot will miss the March release by four weeks.
The loan-system API wasn't ready and I didn't check early enough: that's on me.
Plan: ship the summary panel standalone in March, integrate in April.
Can I count on your support for the standalone release?
you:d18_prewire: Red news, privately, the night before a steering committee: bluff R at its most important.
You assumed an API was ready and did not check.
Owning that plainly to Sarah before the room is the difference between a red project and a broken relationship.
fq:d18_prewire:0: Why am I hearing this the night before?
fa:d18_prewire:0: You're right to ask, and I should have checked the API dependency weeks ago.
I only confirmed it was late this afternoon, and I wanted you to hear it from me before tomorrow rather than in the room.
The plan is solid: the summary panel can ship standalone in March and still save your bankers time, then integrate in April.
Can I count on your support for that tomorrow?
fq:d18_prewire:1: What will you do differently next time?
fa:d18_prewire:1: Check every external dependency in week one, in writing, with the owning team, and recheck it at each milestone.
I assumed the loan-system API was ready because it was on their roadmap, and I didn't verify it.
I've added a dependency check to our project template and asked the API team for a fortnightly status.
It's a simple habit, and I won't skip it again.
set:d18_demo: Your live demo of the summary panel.
cue:d18_demo: The screen freezes on a loading spinner.
you:d18_demo: What twelve people remember is how you handled it.
A light line, a calm switch to the recording, and carrying on, shows the composure that makes executives comfortable putting you in front of their bosses.
Preparation is the backup; presence is the smile.
fq:d18_demo:0: Is it going to do that for my bankers?
fa:d18_demo:0: That freeze was the demo environment's network, not the panel itself, but I won't ask you to take my word for it.
The production version has been running with three bankers for a week, and I'll send you its uptime and response times tonight.
If there's any sign it would freeze for your bankers, we won't release it in March.
You'll have the numbers before you decide.
fq:d18_demo:1: How do you stay calm when a demo breaks?
fa:d18_demo:1: By deciding in advance what I'll do, so there's nothing to decide in the moment.
I always have a recording ready and one light line prepared.
When it breaks, I take a breath, say the line, switch, and keep going.
People take their cue from the presenter: if I panic, they worry; if I'm calm, it's a minor moment.
set:d18_headline: Rehearsal for tonight's dinner with Michael.
model:d18_headline: Kai pushed us to prove AI on a real lending epic: discovery took 6 weeks instead of 14, measured, and every decision is traceable.
you:d18_headline: Under twenty seconds, for the Group Executive, at dinner.
One story, one number, and your sponsor credited first.
This is the compression your feedback asked for, at the highest stakes in the game.
If it takes longer than a breath, cut it.
fq:d18_headline:0: And is it real, or a one-off?
fa:d18_headline:0: Real, and measured on one epic, which is why we're rolling it to four more teams next quarter with the same measures.
Fourteen weeks to six on comparable lending discovery, with fewer review rounds.
One epic isn't a trend yet, and I'd rather say so than overclaim.
Anh Kai set it up so we'd know within a quarter whether it holds across teams.
fa:d18_headline:1: When discovery gets faster, approvals, risk reviews and data access become the slow part.
We saw it in the pilot: data access took longer than the design work.
So scaling isn't just training designers; it's working with Risk to make controls as fast as the work, without weakening them.
That's the harder problem, and the more valuable one to solve.
set:boss_melbourne: A steering committee with a red project, a sceptical GM, a Risk Guardian, and a dinner with the Group Executive.
cue:boss_melbourne: The same person has to show up in all of them.
beat:boss_melbourne:1: Sarah: Honestly, why should I trust an offshore team with my bankers' tools when the dates keep moving?
beat:boss_melbourne:2: Raj: And the AI summaries, how do I know they're right?
beat:boss_melbourne:3: Michael turns to you over the wine.
Kai keeps telling me about you.
beat:boss_melbourne:4: Michael: And what would you do with the whole of Group Digital, if you had it?
beat:boss_melbourne:5: Kai: How did you think that went?
you:boss_melbourne: Melbourne puts every skill in one trip: a red project, a sceptical GM, a Risk Guardian, a dinner with the Group Executive.
Your cross-cultural range is your edge here.
The same person has to show up in every room: honest early, plain English, credit shared, one story with one number.
fq:boss_melbourne:0: So what should I take back to the board?
fa:boss_melbourne:0: One story with one number: a Vietnam team cut lending discovery from fourteen weeks to six, measured, with every decision traceable for Risk.
And one honest caveat: it's one epic, and four more teams next quarter will show whether it scales.
Anh Kai built the conditions for it.
If the board wants, we can show them the decision log; it's the part that makes the speed safe.
fq:boss_melbourne:1: Why should I back your team after a red project?
fa:boss_melbourne:1: Because you heard about the red the night before, from me, with a plan, and the plan is holding.
The usability problem was fixed in a week and the panel ships in March.
A team that tells you bad news early is safer to back than one that only shows green.
I'd like to earn the second pilot with the copilot's results, not ask for it on promises.
brief:19: Now people ask you for sponsorship, and the budget is shrinking.
teach:L19:1: Tier 1, sponsors: every 4-6 weeks: a result, an advice ask, small help.
Tier 2, advocates: monthly or per project.
And every Friday, fifteen minutes: review the log, send one result note and one thanks.
teach:L19:2: If your sponsor gives your idea to someone else to lead: ask what was missing, then supply it, and offer to support.
If you lose a role he backed you for: thank him, ask for the panel's feedback, congratulate the winner publicly.
Sponsors watch how you lose more closely than how you win.
teach:L19:3: Side work, a startup, a contract: declared early under policy, it's a footnote.
If it surfaces and you haven't declared it, fix that immediately with your manager and HR.
cue:d19_map: Sort each person into the tier and cadence they need.
you:d19_map: Head of Design means your network is now your job.
Your relationship log was a tool for one sponsor; now it is a system for dozens of people.
Sorting who needs a monthly touch, who quarterly, and who only when something changes, keeps you reliable at scale.
fq:d19_map:0: How do you keep relationships genuine at this scale?
fa:d19_map:0: By making each touch useful to them, not just regular.
A cadence reminds me when to reconnect; the content has to be real: a result they care about, an introduction, help with a problem.
I keep notes on what each person is focused on, so my message fits their world.
If I have nothing useful, I wait.
A genuine touch every six weeks beats a hollow weekly one.
fq:d19_map:1: Who is easiest to neglect, and why does it matter?
fa:d19_map:1: Senior stakeholders demand attention, so I naturally keep in touch.
But peers like Bao and people I've grown, like Vee, are the ones who shape my reputation day to day and who will be senior themselves in five years.
Neglecting them is how successful people end up isolated.
I'd put a few peers and juniors on a monthly cadence deliberately.
set:d19_sponsee: The cafe downstairs, the same table where you had your first coffee with Kai.
cue:d19_sponsee: I'd like to lead the next pilot.
I think I've shown I can run discovery; I haven't yet shown I can lead the BA and the PO through a hard decision.
Would you back me, and if not yet, what would you need to see?
you:d19_sponsee: Role reversal: Vee makes the ask you made, at the same table.
This is the clearest evidence of all that you have grown someone.
Recognise the craft of her ask, say yes with a condition that grows her gap, and you become the sponsor you once needed.
fq:d19_sponsee:0: What if I mess up the hard decision meeting?
fa:d19_sponsee:0: Then we'll learn from it together, and the project won't suffer, because I'll be in the room.
Messing up a little is part of how you grow into leading.
Before the meeting, we'll prepare the hardest moment together: what you'll do if the PO pushes back.
During it, I'll stay silent unless you ask for help.
You're ready for this, or I wouldn't say yes.
fq:d19_sponsee:1: Why attach a condition to your yes?
fa:d19_sponsee:1: Because a yes without a stretch wastes the opportunity.
Her ask named her gap honestly: leading people through a hard decision.
The condition targets exactly that gap, with a safety net.
It also protects the project and gives me evidence to advocate for her later.
That's what sponsorship is: spending my credibility on her, while making sure she earns it.
It's what Kai did for me.
cue:d19_lost: I've decided Bao will lead the group-wide AI design standard.
you:d19_lost: Losing a lead role you proposed tests whether you are building a career or a grievance.
Your dossier warns about urgency after years of waiting.
Supporting Bao, asking what made him the right choice, and helping him launch it keeps your reputation as someone who puts the work first.
fq:d19_lost:0: Bao has stronger relationships across the platform teams.
fa:d19_lost:0: That makes sense, and it's really useful to know.
Those relationships are exactly what a group-wide standard needs, and I've focused more on delivery than on platform engineering.
I'll work on that: I'd like to spend more time with Chow's teams this quarter.
And I'll help Bao get the standard off the ground; I know the method well.
Thank you for being straight with me.
fq:d19_lost:1: Are you okay with me leading it?
fa:d19_lost:1: I'd be lying if I said I wasn't a little disappointed, but you're a good choice, and your relationships with the platform teams will make it work.
I'd like to help: I can share everything from the pilots, the decision-log templates and the quality gate.
Just tell me where I'm most useful.
A standard that sticks matters more to me than who leads it.
cue:d19_declare: Mate, someone in Group Digital says you're advising an AI startup on the side.
you:d19_declare: Risk H7 in your dossier: outside work surfacing second-hand.
The only safe answer is the true one, already declared and approved.
If your real life matches this scene, the time to check the policy is now, not when someone else asks.
fq:d19_declare:0: Why didn't you tell me about it?
fa:d19_declare:0: You're right, I should have mentioned it to you as a friend, even though it went through the formal process.
I declared it, had it checked against the conflict-of-interest policy, and it's outside work hours with no overlap with the bank's business.
I didn't think to tell people informally, and I see now that it left room for rumours.
I'll send you the approval, and I'm happy to answer anything.
fq:d19_declare:1: Why does declaring matter if the work is harmless?
fa:d19_declare:1: Because harmless and declared are different things to an organisation.
Undeclared outside work, however innocent, looks like hiding when someone else discovers it, and that doubt spreads to everything else I've said.
Declared work is simply a fact.
The policy exists precisely so I don't have to judge conflicts alone.
Checking and declaring early protects my credibility, which is my most valuable asset.
set:d19_talk: Antoine is in the second row.
cue:d19_talk: Make it about what the audience can use, and stay discreet about the bank.
model:d19_talk: Today I want to give you one idea you can try on Monday: put your design decisions in a log the same day you make them.
On one lending epic, my team measured discovery at six weeks instead of fourteen, one epic, so treat it as a strong hint, not a law.
Most of the gain wasn't AI writing things for us.
It was deciding earlier, with everyone looking at the same record.
you:d19_talk: An external talk is visibility beyond the bank, and your strengths as a teacher and mentor shine here.
Two cautions from your dossier: be discreet about the bank, and keep your numbers honest.
Open with one idea the audience can use on Monday.
fq:d19_talk:0: Which bank was that, and can we see the numbers?
fa:d19_talk:0: I'll keep the bank and the details out of a public talk, but I'm happy to share the shape of the method, which is the useful part.
The number came from one epic, measured against a comparable one, so I present it as a strong hint rather than a benchmark.
If you'd like to try the method in your own organisation, I can share a public version of the decision-log template afterwards.
fq:d19_talk:1: Why caveat your own number in front of four hundred people?
fa:d19_talk:1: Because the audience will repeat it, and an unqualified number in a public talk can come back to me and the bank.
Saying one epic, so treat it as a strong hint costs a few seconds and makes me more credible to the people who know measurement.
It's the same habit that worked with Chow: label what's measured and what's estimated, everywhere, including on stage.
set:boss_restructure: Your design org: 24 people across three portfolios.
cue:boss_restructure: We need 10% out of your cost base next year.
Show us how, and how you keep the culture.
beat:boss_restructure:0: Kai: Where does the 10% come from?
beat:boss_restructure:1: Michael: What happens to the craft standard?
beat:boss_restructure:2: Kai: And how do you tell your people?
beat:boss_restructure:3: Bao, on Teams after the meeting: Heard our teams are merging.
you:boss_restructure: A restructure tests whether you can make hard trade-offs across people, the manager evidence your dossier says is thinnest.
Be honest about what you protect and what you spend, protect the culture with process and fairness, and tell people early.
fq:boss_restructure:0: How will you keep the culture through this?
fa:boss_restructure:0: By being honest early, fair in process, and visible.
People will hear the plan from me before any rumours, with the reasons.
Decisions will use clear, consistent criteria, reviewed with HR, so nobody wonders whether it was personal.
And I'll protect the things that make the culture work: the decision logs, the mentoring and the design reviews.
Culture survives hard decisions when people trust how they were made.
fq:boss_restructure:1: What are you giving up that hurts most?
fa:boss_restructure:1: It was where the next generation of method coaches would grow, and losing it slows our scaling by about two quarters.
I chose it over cutting the review practice, because without reviews, AI-speed work becomes risky work.
It's a real cost, and I'll say so openly.
If budget returns, it's the first thing I'd restore, with Vee leading it.
set:trap_leak: Reorg rumours have been everywhere for a week.

What's really happening with Client Platforms?

fq:trap_leak:0: Come on, you must know something about the reorg.
fa:trap_leak:0: I really don't know what has been decided, and even if I had seen something, it would not be mine to share.

If you are worried about your role, let's talk about that properly.
What would make the next month feel more secure for you?
fq:trap_leak:1: Have you been hearing a lot of rumours about the changes?
fa:trap_leak:1: Yes, quite a lot this week, mostly about a merger.
I have not added to them, and when people ask me I tell them I don't know, which is true.
One thing that might help: people are mostly worried about their own roles, not the structure.
If there is a way to share even a rough timeline, I think it would calm things.
I am happy to help shape that message if useful.
brief:20: Michael has a request you shouldn't say yes to.
teach:L20:1: No sponsor is worth your integrity.
Ahn, I don't think I can do that, the board would read it as measured across the portfolio, and it isn't.
Could we show the measured epic big and the estimate labelled?
It gets us most of the way.
If pressed further, the bank's speak-up process exists for exactly this.
The manipulation test: Would I be comfortable if he saw my notes?
Influence helps someone see what is true and useful.
teach:L20:2: Sponsors move: that is why you built three.
Congratulate him genuinely, keep in touch, ask for one introduction to his successor, and strengthen the other relationships.
And when you make a serious mistake: bluff R immediately, then over-deliver on the recovery.

cue:d20_leaves: I'm taking a regional role in Singapore.
I wanted you to hear it from me.
you:d20_leaves: Sponsors move on; the relationship can outlast the role.
Your dossier says sponsorship is a long game.
Congratulate Kai sincerely, thank him for telling you first, and ask for an introduction to his successor.
fq:d20_leaves:0: Will you be okay without me here?
fa:d20_leaves:0: I think so, ahn, largely because of what you've helped me build: the team, the evidence and the relationships with Sarah, Raj and Michael.
I'll miss your advice, though, and I'd love to keep in touch properly, perhaps a call every couple of months.
And if anything I'm doing could help your new team in Singapore, I'd be glad to.
fq:d20_leaves:1: Why ask for an introduction to his successor?
fa:d20_leaves:1: Because a new leader inherits a team with no context about who does what.
An introduction from Kai gives me a warm start and some of his credibility, instead of starting cold.
